packs.title: Collections, habitats and open paths
packs.promise: Read local records, look closely at habitats and make something on an open path.

q.s: Build a small reading trail from an actual public collection.
st: Choose a question you would like to investigate, then find three actual books in an open public shelf area that approach it from different angles.
For each book, record its actual title and author or other stated creator, plus a shelf label, call number or visible contents topic that helped you find it. Do not copy long passages.
Write one different question you would ask of each book. A title or contents page can guide the question; reading all three books is unnecessary.
Put the three short records in the order you might explore them and explain the first choice in one sentence. Return books as staff direct rather than guessing their shelf positions.

q.s: Record a wetland’s forms without collecting its wildlife.
st: Follow the current IRWD map to an open portion of Fledgling Loop near the visitor campus and ponds A and B. Choose a short comfortable return rather than a whole-marsh circuit.

Collect three written edge records: where open water meets vegetation, where a path meets planting, and where a nearer form overlaps a farther one. If water is obscured, record that actual view instead of inventing a shoreline.
For each, describe one visible shape, colour or texture. Wildlife sightings and species identification are unnecessary.
Add the operator’s urban-runoff-treatment fact to your notes with its source named. Keep that sourced purpose separate from the three things you observed.

q.s: Collect three ways a park frames its water.
st: Choose an open developed-park path with a view of the lake, keeping away from closed work areas and the water edge.
Collect three actual framing details: a path bend, planted edge, seat, tree line or opening that changes the view toward water. Use only what is present.
For each detail, write where it directs your attention and one visible effect, such as a wider view, a partly hidden edge or a nearer foreground. Do not infer the designer’s intention as fact.
Make a three-row park-view record. Add your own question about which detail helps you stop and look.

packs.title: Great Park in two afternoons
packs.promise: Follow two connected afternoons of gardens, aviation, art and open park views.

q.s: Use a demonstration garden’s actual labels to start a growing notebook.
st: Enter the open visitor garden and choose three actual labelled demonstration beds or planting areas. Keep to the visitor path.
For each, record a stated theme or plant name and one visible growing detail, such as support, spacing, container, mulch or growth form. Do not infer a plant’s identity without its label.
Write a practical question for each example about growing in a small space. Mark questions as your own rather than treating them as garden instructions.
Arrange the three records as a small growing notebook and choose which question you would investigate first. Nothing needs to be picked or tasted.

q.s: Check how an actual exhibition uses different forms.
st: Enter the open Gallery and choose three currently displayed examples that use different forms, such as a publication, graphic item, image, map or sound interpretation. Use the forms actually available today.
For each, record an actual label identifier or displayed title and one visible design detail. If a listening station is unavailable, a readable interpretation panel can supply the third record.
Write one question about what each form makes easy to share or notice. Keep the question as your response rather than attributing it to an artist.
Make three short media cards, separating label facts, visible design observations and your own questions. Avoid copying a long lyric, publication page or protected image.

q.s: Turn repeated shapes in a plaza into six original lines.
st: Find three actual repetitions or contrasts in the plaza: a trunk line, leaf shape, shade patch, pavement edge or opening between palms. Cloudy light and still palms work too.
Assign each detail an invented written sound, rhythm or short phrase. Do not describe imagined music as something you heard in the park.
Write a quiet six-line score or stanza using the three details in an order of your choice. Keep it on the page; no public performance is needed.
Add three margin notes linking your words to the real plaza observations. Give the piece an original title.
